text: Before judging whether a quantum approach helps, you need a crisp, shared picture of what classical machine learning already does well. This lesson recaps the core classical pipeline so every later comparison to a quantum version has a fair, specific baseline.

Nearly every classifier follows the same shape. Features turn raw data into a numeric vector x. A model, a weighted sum, a decision tree, a neural network, or later a quantum circuit, maps those features to a prediction. A loss function measures how wrong the predictions are. And an optimizer, almost always some form of gradient descent, adjusts the model's parameters to reduce that loss.

Here's gradient descent worked by hand. With loss equal to theta minus 3, squared, starting at theta equals zero with a learning rate of 0.1, the gradient is negative 6, pushing theta up to 0.6 on the first step. One more step, using the new gradient of negative 4.8, lands at 1.08. This exact update rule trains a variational quantum circuit's parameters in Chapter 2 — only how the gradient itself gets computed will change, using the parameter-shift rule instead of backpropagation.

A linear classifier draws a straight boundary, predicting one class if w dot x plus b is positive. The kernel trick computes a similarity value, k of x and x prime, directly, without ever building the higher-dimensional mapping phi of x explicitly. This is the exact structure Chapter 3's quantum kernels borrow: a quantum circuit computes that similarity measure, and everything else in the support vector machine around it stays completely classical.
Next lesson introduces the two real, actively maintained libraries, PennyLane and Qiskit Machine Learning, that every circuit, gradient, and training loop in this course actually runs through.
